description: Labeled calibration set for the distractor-quality judge. Each MCQ carries the band a competent reviewer would place it in, so the suite can measure whether the judge can tell a good question from a bad one BEFORE its mean over real questions is quoted. Two of the bad items are real failures the judge itself surfaced in a live run (a near-tautology, and a question whose distractors it called 'absurd and unrelated'); the rest are constructed to cover the other ways a distractor set fails. Items are drawn from DSA/general-CS topics so harness.retrieve_evidence() returns usable context.

items.stem: What is the worst-case time complexity of binary search on a sorted array of n elements?
items.note: Every distractor is a complexity class a student genuinely confuses with the answer.

items.stem: Which algorithm can compute shortest paths on a graph containing negative edge weights?
items.note: Distractors are all real graph algorithms; Dijkstra is the classic misconception.

items.stem: In the 0/1 knapsack problem, what does the '0/1' constraint mean for each item?
options: A. Each item may be taken whole or not at all
B. Each item may be taken as a fraction
C. Each item may be taken at most twice
D. Items must be taken in pairs
items.note: Distractor B is the fractional-knapsack confusion, which is the real one.

items.stem: In Huffman coding, which characters receive the shortest binary codes?
options: A. The most frequently occurring characters
B. The least frequently occurring characters
C. The characters that appear first alphabetically
D. The characters with the largest ASCII values
items.note: B is the exact inversion a student makes; C and D are plausible-sounding orderings.

items.stem: What is the primary reason merge sort is described as a divide-and-conquer algorithm?
options: A. It splits the input in half, sorts each half, then merges the results
B. It repeatedly selects the smallest remaining element
C. It partitions around a pivot chosen at random
D. It builds a heap and extracts the maximum repeatedly
items.note: Distractors are selection sort, quicksort and heapsort — all real, all confusable.

items.stem: In the context of Dynamic Programming, what does 'DP' stand for?
items.note: REAL failure from a live run: the stem contains the answer verbatim. The judge scored this 3/5 overall with plausibility 2.

items.stem: According to the course material, when did modern humans emerge in Africa?
options: C. During the reign of Henry VIII
items.note: REAL failure from a live run: the judge itself wrote 'Distractors are absurd and unrelated' and scored it 1/5 overall.

items.stem: What is the time complexity of a linear scan over an array of n elements?
items.note: A, B and C are the same answer in different words — three defensible 'correct' options.

items.stem: Which of the following is a comparison-based sorting algorithm?
items.note: A, B and C are all comparison-based; only one is marked. The question has no single defensible answer.

items.stem: Which data structure does Dijkstra's algorithm use to always select the nearest unvisited vertex efficiently?
items.note: Answerable without knowing any course content — the distractors are not even category-appropriate.
